clinicalPearls: Represents acquired heterotopic autotransplantation of splenic pulp after splenic rupture or splenectomy, with implants seeding peritoneal and serosal surfaces and acquiring a new blood supply

Distinguished from an accessory spleen, which is congenital, usually solitary and near the hilum, possesses a hilum and is supplied by the splenic artery, whereas splenosis is acquired, multiple, lacks a hilum and parasitises surrounding vessels
Thoracic splenosis follows combined splenic and left diaphragmatic injury, producing left pleural-based nodules that can mimic malignancy
Usually asymptomatic and found incidentally, but can be mistaken for peritoneal metastases, carcinomatosis, mesothelioma, lymphoma or endometriosis
Technetium-labelled heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy, ideally with SPECT/CT, confirms functioning splenic tissue and averts unnecessary biopsy or surgery
Implants restore only partial splenic function, so vaccination and infection prophylaxis appropriate to hyposplenism should still be considered
Disappearance of Howell-Jolly bodies from the blood film after splenectomy can be a clue to functioning splenosis
Implants can be found throughout the abdomen and pelvis, and rarely in the thorax, liver or subcutaneous tissue at old wound sites
reference.pathophysiology: Splenosis develops when splenic pulp is disseminated during traumatic rupture or at splenectomy, seeding the peritoneal cavity, omentum, serosal surfaces of the bowel, mesentery and diaphragm, or the pleural space when the diaphragm is breached. The viable red pulp fragments implant on vascularised surfaces and induce neovascularisation, deriving a blood supply from the surrounding host tissue rather than from the splenic artery. The resulting nodules are histologically splenic and retain some filtering and immune capacity, but their total mass and disordered architecture usually provide only incomplete restoration of splenic function. Because they enlarge slowly and appear as multiple soft-tissue nodules, they frequently masquerade radiologically as metastatic or peritoneal malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Pleural tumour or metastasis in thoracic splenosis
Hepatic adenoma or focal lesion when intrahepatic
additionalInvestigations: Technetium heat-damaged red cell or sulphur-colloid scintigraphy with SPECT/CT
Contrast-enhanced CT to map the nodules and their distribution
MRI, including superparamagnetic iron oxide-enhanced sequences exploiting reticuloendothelial uptake
Full blood count and peripheral blood film for Howell-Jolly bodies and other hyposplenic features
Documentation of prior splenic trauma or splenectomy in the history
Image-guided biopsy only where the diagnosis remains genuinely uncertain
redFlags: Imaging features that cannot confidently be distinguished from malignancy and require exclusion
Gastrointestinal bleeding or bowel obstruction attributable to an implant
Haemoptysis or pleuritic symptoms in thoracic splenosis
reference.prognosis: Splenosis is benign and the great majority of patients remain asymptomatic for life, needing no treatment. The principal hazard is misdiagnosis as malignancy leading to unnecessary intervention.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting implants as malignancy and proceeding to needless biopsy or resection
Assuming splenosis fully restores immune function and omitting vaccination and prophylaxis
Not considering the diagnosis in a patient with prior splenic trauma and new peritoneal or pleural nodules
Confusing splenosis with a congenital accessory spleen
management: No treatment for asymptomatic splenosis, which is benign and requires only recognition
Confirm the diagnosis non-invasively with technetium heat-damaged red cell scintigraphy, ideally with SPECT/CT, to avoid unnecessary biopsy or surgery
Avoid resection or biopsy unless the diagnosis remains genuinely uncertain or implants become symptomatic through pain, bleeding or obstruction
Because implants restore only partial splenic function, consider vaccination and infection prophylaxis appropriate to hyposplenism
Monitor the peripheral blood film for hyposplenic features such as Howell-Jolly bodies to gauge residual splenic function
Reserve surgical excision for genuinely symptomatic implants or complications
